title: How To Introduce Units Of Study And Set Your Students On Fire For Learning ur-students-on-fire-for-learning/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin advocates opening new units of study with storytelling instead of a traditional preview or introductory lesson. He argues teachers should mine their topic for its human drama—characters, tension, setbacks, and victories—and deliver it as a narrative rather than a list of facts. Using the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb as an example, he offers tips for effective delivery: staying in storytelling mode rather than sliding into fact-listing, acting out key moments, being authentic rather than polished, and finding creative angles even for seemingly dry subjects. He argues storytelling fits any curriculum, including Common Core, and deepens engagement, comprehension, and emotional investment from the very first lesson of a unit.
points: Opening a new unit with a narrative story, rather than a traditional preview, is presented as a way to dramatically boost interest and retention.
Teachers should mine their topic for genuine human drama—characters, tension, setbacks, and victories—before crafting the story.
Delivery tips include staying in storytelling mode rather than lapsing into fact-lists, and acting out key scenes with voice and movement.
The strategy is described as flexible enough to fit any standards or curriculum, including Common Core.
A well-told opening story is credited with making subsequent lessons in the unit easier to deliver, since students become emotionally invested early.
quotes: There exists an amazing strategy that will dramatically increase student interest, motivation, and comprehension in virtually whatever you’re studying.

The way it works is that instead of giving your students a preview of what they’re about to learn, instead of reading an introduction or teaching a more traditional first lesson . . . you will tell a story.
There once was a man named Howard Carter who spent six years searching for the lost tomb of a boy king.
Be careful not to get sidetracked writing out lists of facts or key points for your students.
Storytelling is the most flexible and dynamic medium available to teachers, and it will fit seamlessly into whatever standards or curriculum you’ve been asked to follow
